keyVerseText: Even so would he have removed thee out of the strait into a broad place, where there is no straitness; and that which should be set on thy table should be full of fatness. that: Heb. the rest of thy table
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun מוּצַק (mûwtsaq) derives from the root יָצַק (yâtsaq), which fundamentally means to pour out or cast, often in the context of molten metal solidifying into a firm shape. This root conveys the idea of something being made firm, set, or hardened. Thus, מוּצַק carries the literal sense of constraint or narrowness as if something is tightly cast or pressed, adding a physical dimension of restriction beyond the general English ideas of distress or anguish.
usageInScripture: The word מוּצַק appears three times in Scripture, each time conveying a sense of constraint or distress. Its translations range from 'there is no straitness' to 'is straitened' and 'shall not be such as was in her vexation,' indicating both the presence and removal of distress or narrowness. This consistency in usage underscores its thematic role in describing situations of limitation or hardship, often contrasted with relief or broadness.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מוּצַק enriches our grasp of the biblical portrayal of human affliction and divine deliverance. The image of being 'cast' or 'pressed' into narrowness reflects the reality of trials and constraints believers face, yet it also points to God's power to reshape and set firm what is fragile. The tension between distress and relief in this term mirrors the Christian journey of suffering and hope, reminding us that God can transform our straitness into a place of spiritual broadness and abundance.
keyVerseReflection: In Job 36:16, the phrase 'there is no straitness' uses מוּצַק to highlight God's deliverance from distress into a place of freedom and blessing. The verse promises removal from the 'strait' and provision of abundance, emphasizing that God not only rescues from constraint but also enriches the believer's life. This word vividly captures the transition from hardship to divine grace, encouraging trust in God's sustaining care.
